title: Orders, Leverage & the Mechanics
promise: How a trade is actually placed, and the one tool that turns small mistakes into account-killers.
unlock: Pick the right order and set a stop-loss the moment you trade
Profit from falls as well as rises (and know the risk)
Work out what leverage really does to your money
Spot the four costs nobody advertises
Size a trade so an overnight gap can’t knock you out

questions.q: You buy at $30. You want out automatically if it falls to $27. Which order?
questions.why: A sell stop below the price waits and fires only if it falls to $27. A sell limit means “$27 or better”, so it would sell now at $30. A buy limit buys.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

chart.label: You bought at $30; the $27 level sits below the price

questions.q: You short 200 shares at $25 and buy them back at $22. Ignoring costs, what’s your result?
questions.why: A short gains when the price falls. You sold high and bought back lower, so you made money.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

chart.label: Shorted at $25, the price falls and you buy back at $22

questions.q: You put $500 in at 20× leverage. How big is the position, and what move wipes you out?
questions.why: $500 × 20 = $10,000 position. At 20×, a 5% move against you (100% ÷ 20) costs $500, your whole margin.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

questions.q: You buy and sell 100 shares once. Broker A: $0 commission, $0.05 spread. Broker B: $1 per trade, $0.01 spread. Which is cheaper?
questions.why: Add both costs. A: $0.05 spread × 100 shares = $5. B: $1 × 2 trades = $2 commission + $0.01 × 100 = $1 spread, $3 total.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

questions.q: Your account is $10,000 and you risk 1% on a stock that often gaps 10% on news. What’s the largest sensible position?
questions.why: 1% of $10,000 = $100 you can risk. A 10% gap should cost no more than that: $100 ÷ 10% = $1,000 position.
questions.added: New situation written for the Academy

chart.label: Two overnight gaps of about 10%, one down and one up

retry.q: A stock trades at $80. You want to buy it only if it dips to $75. Which order?
retry.why: A buy limit waits below the price: “$75 or less”. A buy stop at $75 fires right away, since the price is already above it. A market order buys now at $80.
retry.added: New situation written for the Academy

chart.label: The price is at $80, above a $75 level

retry.q: You short 100 shares at $50. The price rises and you buy them back at $56. Ignoring costs, what’s your result?
retry.why: A short loses when the price rises. You sold at $50 and had to buy back higher, so every share cost you more than you got.
retry.added: New situation written for the Academy

chart.label: Shorted at $50, the price rises and you buy back at $56

retry.q: You put $2,000 into a forex trade at 50× leverage. How big is the position, and what move wipes you out?
retry.why: Position = margin × leverage. The move that takes all your margin is 100% ÷ leverage, and a margin call comes even earlier.
retry.added: New situation written for the Academy

retry.q: You buy and sell 200 shares once. Broker A: $0 commission, $0.04 spread. Broker B: $2 per trade, $0.01 spread. Which is cheaper?
retry.why: Add both costs: commission on each trade plus the spread on every share. A’s wider spread costs more than B’s fees.
retry.work: A: $0.04 × 200 shares = $8. B: $2 × 2 trades = $4 commission + $0.01 × 200 = $2 spread, $6 total.
retry.added: New situation written for the Academy

retry.q: Your account is $20,000 and you risk 1%. The stock can gap 20% on earnings. What’s the largest sensible position?
retry.why: Size for the gap, not the stop: your risk budget divided by the gap gives the largest position.
retry.added: New situation written for the Academy

refresher.title: Lesson 1 · The four orders you’ll use 95% of the time
refresher.text: A limit waits for your price or better: a buy limit sits below the price. A stop waits for the price to reach a level, then trades: a sell stop below the price is your stop-loss.

refresher.title: Lesson 2 · Long and short
refresher.text: A short sells first and buys back later. Profit is (sell − buy) × shares. Short 50 at $40 and buy back at $34? You gain $300.

refresher.title: Lesson 3 · Leverage, the double-edged sword
refresher.text: Position = margin × leverage. The move against you that takes all your margin = 100% ÷ leverage: 10× → 10%, 100× → 1%. A margin call comes even earlier.

refresher.title: Lesson 4 · The costs nobody advertises
refresher.text: Add every cost before you compare: commission on each trade plus the spread on every share of every round trip. Zero commission with a wide spread can cost more.

refresher.title: Lesson 5 · The overnight gamble
refresher.text: A gap can jump your stop, so size is your protection. Risk 1% of the account, then divide by the typical gap. $5,000 × 1% = $50, and $50 ÷ 10% = $500.
